steps.text: here's the idea behind the name hey you.
researchers asked people to give a speech with almost no time to prepare. before it, some talked to themselves as "i". others used "you" or their own name.
the "you" group gave better speeches, saw the task more as a challenge than a threat, and dwelled on it less afterward.
these studies come from ethan kross's lab at the university of michigan. the paper, published in 2014, reports seven experiments.
why do you think that helps?

options.label: it's like a friend talking
options.reply: exactly. it gives you the distance you'd have with a friend's problem.

options.label: it feels a bit weird
options.reply: it can, at first. weird and useful can be the same thing.

options.label: not sure
options.reply: it gives you a little distance, the way you'd see a friend's problem more clearly than your own.

steps.text: hey {name}, you've handled hard weeks before.

ideas: can take this one step at a time.
have gotten through hard days before.
don't have to figure it all out tonight.

steps.text: talking to yourself as "you" gives you the distance you'd give a friend.
next time something's hard, say one sentence to yourself using "you" or your name. out loud, if you can.

grounding.idea: talking to yourself as "you" or by name reduced anxiety and rumination under stress
grounding.source: Kross et al., 2014, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
